business_type_notes: The pack's section 2 has one GBP category, Pest control service, and keeps it type A throughout, so category_types is empty and the one category page reads the A briefs. Urgent against planned is split by page, not by category: the library's emergency column (Wasp nest removal, Rat and mouse control, with Drain inspections for rodents as an alias of the second) switches the emergency variant on when the client confirms call outs; every other page gets the plain briefs, and a client with no call outs gets the plain briefs on those two pages as well (the pack: emergency language only where call outs are confirmed). Inside the planned pages the pack's registers are carried in the card briefs: problem led (the sign the customer sees, the pest behind it, the way in and what stops the return) for bed bugs, ants, cockroaches, fleas, squirrels, moles, rabbits, foxes and wildlife, moths and textile pests, woodworm, insect control, dead animal removal, loft clearance and decontamination, fumigation and heat treatment, and for pest surveys and inspections at a home (an investigation register: what the survey settles); schedule led (what slips and when, with the reason in the site and the season, and what an inspector expects on paper) for Commercial pest control and for surveys and monitoring at a business; no desire led page: the pack's section 2 lists none (pest proofing is problem led and commercial is schedule led), so the library's desire_led column is blank throughout and there is no desire variant; the proofing, bird and commercial pages read the planned block 4 with their own lines in its briefs. Bee removal and relocation is confirm_only in the library and keeps the pack's angle (which bee it is, and why honey bees are moved rather than destroyed) inside the planned card briefs; the briefs never write a legal bee protection, because the trade facts record none. Nothing here is a type B diary round in the template's sense: a commercial contract is a schedule led page under type A, as the pack has it, so there is no B entry; a client set to B by hand would find no briefs and should be set back to A. Seasonal: wasp nests run mainly spring to autumn and the colony abandons the nest in autumn, honey bee swarms come in late spring and early summer, ant activity shows more in warm months and rodent activity indoors shows more in the cold months (Table A timing cells), so seasonal_trade is on and the seasonal swap carries that with the reason in the animal's year, never a busy season.

steps.title: Tell Us What You've Seen or Heard
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to say first: what they have seen or heard (droppings, scratching, insects going in and out of one spot, bites, holes in timber or in clothes) and where and when (at night, in the daytime, in the loft, behind the cooker, under the floor); whether anyone in the house reacts badly to stings; whether there are pets or small children, because that shapes what is used and where (the trade facts: bait kept from children and animals that are not the target, hosts treated separately for fleas); a photo taken from a distance if it is safe, since the insect or animal is identified before anything is treated (Table E: a cluster of honey bees can be a swarm, not a wasp nest). Nothing from the shop meanwhile, with the reason from Table B only: a nest disturbed without proper control means more stings, trails treated without the colony leave the source, bait left in the open puts pets and other animals at risk. Never how to use any product. No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Identify the Pest and Price the Job
steps.brief: The visit and what gets looked at: which insect or animal it is (every Table A row starts there: wasp against bee, rat against mouse, active against historic woodworm), where it lives and how it gets in (harbourage, food, water and entry points; the drain where rat entry is suspected; the roof line and the vents for squirrels and birds), and what has to be weighed before anything is used (children, pets, other animals, a protected animal or a nest in use, access and height). Then the price. On a survey page the survey is the job that is priced, and any treatment is priced off what it finds. Follows [CV: quote_method]; only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps.title: We Treat It and Deal With the Way In
steps.brief: The date is agreed in advance, to suit the customer. What the visit does only from the Table A stages for that pest, in plain words: traps or protected bait points for rodents, the nest treated at its entrance, a treatment or heat for bed bugs, bait the ants carry back to the colony; a follow up visit written as part of the method with its reason in the animal (eggs, pupae or egg cases that a treatment does not reach; traps and bait points that are checked and cleared), never as a fixed number of visits (Table G: none exists); proofing as the last stage where the services list has it, otherwise recommended. Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan (step 2 and Why choose us own them). Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it). Never a promise the pest will not return.

step_2_no_visit.title: We Price Your Job
step_2_no_visit.brief: Say a price is agreed before any work starts. Describe how the price is reached only from [CV: quote_method]; when quote_method is blank, name no method at all (no photos, call, video or visit). The insect or animal is still identified on the first visit before anything is used (Table A). Only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps_emergency.title: Call Us
steps_emergency.brief: What to say: what they have seen (a stream of wasps at one spot by a door, a window or where children play; a rat or a mouse seen indoors; droppings in the kitchen), where it is, whether anyone in the house reacts badly to stings, whether there are pets or small children. What to do meanwhile, from the trade facts rows only: keep people and pets away from a nest entrance and leave it alone (Table B: an occupied nest disturbed without proper control means more stings); put food away in sealed containers and clear what has been gnawed (Table B: accessible food keeps rodents active); nothing laid or sprayed from the shop (Table B: exposed bait puts pets and other animals at risk; a body left behind a wall is the smell they fear). Never an instruction to go into the loft or up a ladder. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps_emergency.title: We Come Out, Identify It and Agree the Price
steps_emergency.brief: What usually happens first on the visit, from Table A: the insect or animal confirmed before anything is used (Table E: a cluster of honey bees can be a swarm, and treating the wrong insect harms bees), the nest or the activity located and its exposure assessed, who is at risk and how access is made safe. The customer told what was found. A call out charge only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee]; the price agreed before any treatment only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]. An arrival time only as the business gives it on the call: no window written here unless [CV: response_time] is set; 'same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes. Never restates 'free'.

steps_emergency.title: We Treat It, Then Close the Way In
steps_emergency.brief: What the visit does, from Table A: a wasp nest treated at its entrance with access made safe and people kept clear, the activity checked afterwards and the empty nest removed only if needed; for rats and mice, traps or protected bait points where justified, follow up visits to check them and to remove spent bait and bodies, then the entry points proofed (Table A stages; Table C: bait points protected, recorded and cleared at the end, as what the professional usually does, never the code's name). The follow up is part of the method with its reason in the animal, never a fixed number of visits. Never promise a one visit fix; never mention the price; never a promise the pest will not return.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Used only when a guarantee or manufacturer warranty is confirmed. Start with yes, then the terms from the client values. A guarantee is the client's own written terms (Table E: consumer law asks for reasonable care and skill, not a promise that no pest ever returns), so it is described, with its length and what it covers as given, and never written as the pest never coming back.

faq_slots.question: What happens if the pests come back after treatment?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Used when nothing in cover_chain other than insurance is confirmed. Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the honest reasons a pest shows again, from the trade facts: eggs, pupae or egg cases that sit out a treatment and emerge afterwards (Table E: fleas seen after treatment do not on their own show the treatment failed), which is why a follow up is part of the method, or a way in that was never closed, which is why proofing follows a rodent treatment. Then the 'reasonable care and skill' standard every trade works to, as the standard the work is held to, never as a defence. No promise to come back or treat again for free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: How do your quotes work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] only. A call out charge only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee].

faq_slots.question: What about my children and pets while the house is being treated?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Never 'safe for pets and children' or any version of it: a claim. What the professional usually does, from the Table C and E rows as what usually applies and never the code's or an Act's name: bait in protected points out of reach, the points recorded and checked, bodies and spilled bait collected, uneaten bait removed when the treatment ends; a product used only as its label allows. What the customer is asked to do during and after a treatment only as it is given on the day for that job (Table C: the re entry and access restrictions for the particular job), so name no time out of the room. For fleas, the pet is treated separately through the vet (Table A: animal hosts treated separately). Never a product named.

faq_slots.question: What is making the scratching noise in my loft?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Help the reader narrow it down from the Table B signs rows, in plain words and never as certain from the sound alone: scratching in the walls or overhead once the house is quiet with droppings and gnawed packaging points to rats or mice; scratching in the daytime with disturbed insulation and damaged vents points more to grey squirrels; birds under the eaves bring nesting material and droppings below. Bats are protected and a roost means advice, never a treatment (Table C and E, as what usually applies, never the Act). Then that whichever it is, there is a way in, at the roof line, a vent or an air brick (Table A: entry points located, closed after exclusion). Then what the local housing adds (connected roof spaces on older terraces, trees close to the roofs), as the research gives it, never as the current state of anyone's home. Then what finding it involves: the survey, and the way in closed only once the animals are out (Table B: sealing before they are out traps them).

faq_slots.question: Do I have to tell the council or my landlord?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts rule rows only, written as what usually applies and never with an Act's or a regulation's name: an occupier who knows rats or mice are living on the land in substantial numbers usually has to tell the council in writing (Table C), which is about rats and mice in numbers, not every mouse and not bed bugs (Table E); a tenant tells the landlord about a problem, and who pays depends on the cause and the tenancy, with no rule that either side always pays (Table E). Council treatment and charges vary by area, so never 'the council does it free' (Table E). Never legal advice.

faq_slots.question: Will one visit be enough?
faq_slots.answer_brief: It depends on the pest and the method, from the Table A and E rows: a wasp nest is treated at its entrance and the activity checked afterwards; rats and mice need follow up visits to check the traps or the bait points, remove spent bait and bodies, then proofing; fleas, bed bugs and cockroaches have eggs, pupae or egg cases that a treatment does not reach, so monitoring and a follow up are part of the method and a flea seen afterwards is usually a newly emerged one, not a failed treatment. Never a fixed number of visits (Table G: none is established); never a promise it ends with one.

faq_slots.question: Does bird proofing need permission?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": netting, spikes or mesh on an ordinary house usually need no permission; on a listed building a fixture that affects its character usually needs consent first; a nest in use is protected whenever it is in use, with no calendar date, so the work is timed around it. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it. No figure, never an Act's or a licence's name.

Rodents: drain camera check for rat entry
Proofing: vent grilles that keep the airflow
Wildlife: specialist mole gassing by a certificated operator

cards.title: Scratching you hear after dark, or in the day
cards.brief: Problem led, the pack's planned register: what they hear and when, from the Table B signs rows: scratching in the walls or above a bedroom ceiling at night with droppings and gnawed packaging below (rats and mice); scratching in the loft in the daytime with disturbed insulation and a damaged vent (grey squirrels); nesting material and droppings under the eaves (birds). The one cause this card makes: an animal that has found a gap into the roof or the floor void. Help the reader narrow it down without making it certain from the sound alone; say what finding it involves from Table A: the species confirmed, the loft and the roof access inspected, a check for protected wildlife before anything is done (bats and a roost are advice, never a treatment; a nest in use is protected whenever it is in use: Table C and E, as what usually applies and never the Act), then traps or protected bait where justified for rodents, cage traps for squirrels, and the entry closed only once the animals are out (Table B: sealing first traps them). A captured grey squirrel is not released (Table E), said plainly as the law the trade works to, never the order's name. What it leads to if left, from the skipped rows: gnawed cables and insulation, young born in the loft. Never a scare; never 'infestation'.
cards.mechanism: an animal that has found a gap into the roof or the floor void

cards.title: Droppings under the sink or along a skirting
cards.brief: Problem led: droppings near food or the bins, gnawed packaging, holes round the pipes, a urine smell (Table B rat and mouse signs). The one cause this card makes: food and warmth within reach of an opening low down or in the drains: a hole where a pipe comes through, a broken air brick, a failed joint in an older drain that lets rats up into the floor void (Table E: rats can travel through drains). Say what the fix usually involves from Table A: the species identified, harbourage, food and entry points located, a plan that weighs children, pets and other animals, traps or protected bait points where justified, follow up to check them and remove spent bait and bodies, then the entry points proofed with mesh and cement; a drain camera where drain entry is suspected and a one way valve only where it fits, never as compulsory (Table E). The stewardship as what the professional usually does (Table C), never the code's name. Where rats or mice are there in numbers, the occupier usually has to tell the council in writing (Table C, with 'usually'). Rodents can carry disease: said once and plainly, never a statistic (the pack's craft rule). Never DIY poison, never shame.
cards.mechanism: food and warmth within reach of an opening low down or in the drains

cards.title: Wasps, bees or ants going in at one spot
cards.brief: Problem led: wasps in and out of one hole under the eaves or in the brickwork, bees entering a cavity or clustered on a branch, ants in a line to food with small soil pellets at an entrance (Table B signs). The one cause this card makes: a colony living inside the fabric of the house or the ground, with its entrance where the traffic shows. Which insect it is decides everything (Table E: species identified before treatment; a cluster of honey bees may be a swarm). Wasps: the nest located, its exposure assessed, treatment at the entrance with a professional product chosen for the nest position, never named, the activity checked and the empty nest removed only if needed (Table A); a low risk nest in autumn may be left, since the colony abandons it (Table E). Bees: honey bees usually referred to a beekeeper where a swarm can be collected, a settled colony inside a wall needing the comb dealt with as well, bumblebee nests usually left because they finish by autumn, treatment only as a last resort (Table A and E); never 'all bees are protected' (Table E records no such law). Ants: the trail traced to the nest and a bait the workers carry back, since treating the trail alone leaves the colony, and some species spread into new nests when disturbed, which is why identification comes first (Table A and B). Never a product, never how to use a shop spray. Urgent nests by a door go to the emergency variant where it is on.
cards.mechanism: a colony living inside the fabric of the house, with its entrance where the traffic is

cards.title: Bites, and insects you only see at night
cards.brief: Problem led: bites noticed after sleep with spotting at the mattress seams and cast skins (bed bugs); bites round the ankles, insects where a pet rests, activity after vacuuming (fleas); insects seen when a light goes on, around warm appliances, egg cases in cracks (cockroaches) (Table B signs). The one cause this card makes: eggs, pupae or egg cases in the fabric of the room that an incomplete treatment does not reach, so the numbers come back (Table B skipped rows). Say what the fix involves from Table A: inspection and identification, the harbourages and rooms mapped, contents prepared, a residual treatment or specialist heat or steam for bed bugs, pets treated separately through the vet and floors vacuumed for fleas, gel bait and monitors with harbourages sealed for cockroaches, then monitoring and a follow up where surviving stages emerge (Table E: a flea seen after treatment is usually newly emerged, not a failed job). A follow up as part of the method, never a fixed number of visits (Table G). Why the shop attempt fell short only as Table B states it (eggs that survive an incomplete intervention). Never shame, never 'dirty', never a product.
cards.mechanism: eggs, pupae or egg cases that an incomplete treatment never reaches

faq_symptom.frame: [SYMPTOM]: why does it happen, and what can be done?
faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom and its linked local issue, answered as asked. Where the symptom is a seasonal sign (wasps gone quiet in autumn, a flea seen after a treatment, rodents heard as the nights draw in), say first when it is normal and then what is not, before anything else. problem_card.title: Rodents moving indoors as the nights turn cold
problem_card.brief: Say first what is normal at the turn of the year: wasps gone quiet and a nest found in winter usually empty, since the colony abandons it in autumn (Table A and E); ants not seen until the weather warms (Table A). Then what is not: scratching that starts as the nights draw in, droppings where there were none, gnawed packets in a cupboard. The one cause this card makes: the cold pushing rats and mice in to where there is warmth and food (Table A rat and mouse timing: indoor activity more apparent in colder weather). Say what gets looked at from Table A: the way in (pipes, air bricks, the roof line, the drain), food within reach, then traps or protected bait where justified and the proofing that follows; the farmland edge of town only where the town profile gives it. Nothing about autumn being busy or booking ahead; no dates.
problem_card.mechanism: the cold pushing rats and mice in to where there is warmth and food

faq_slot.question: Do you still deal with wasp nests in the autumn and winter?
faq_slot.answer_brief: From the Table A and E rows: wasp work runs mainly from spring to autumn; the colony abandons the nest in autumn, so a nest found in winter usually needs nothing, and a low risk nest can be left alone; what matters in the cold months is the rodent side, since indoor activity shows more in colder weather. Said with the reason in the animal's year, never as a busy or a quiet season. No dates.

cost.h2: What Moves the Price of an Emergency Call Out in [CITY]

cards.title: When you call
cards.brief: The time of day and the day of the week move the price: an evening or a weekend call for a nest by the back door against a weekday morning. A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; never say there is no charge for coming out unless [CV: quote_call_out_fee] says there is none. Whether the business comes out at those hours only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; when it is not set, nothing about hours at all. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting to the nest or the run
cards.brief: How far the house is from the base and what it takes to reach the problem once there: a nest under the eaves three storeys up or inside a cavity, a loft with no boards, a run behind fitted units, a flat roof with no ladder access (Table F wasp nest removal: nest height, concealed location, special access equipment; Table F rat and mouse control: the number of rooms or buildings). Distance and access move the price; say why in plain words. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; never hours of cover unless [CV: out_of_hours_available] says so.

cards.title: Finding it and dealing with it on the day
cards.brief: What is done first on a call out, from Table A: wasps confirmed rather than bees before anything is used (Table E: a cluster of honey bees can be a swarm), the nest found and how exposed it is judged, people and pets kept clear and access made safe, then the nest treated at its entrance; for rats and mice the species confirmed, the runs, the food and the ways in found, and traps or protected bait points set where justified. How long that takes is what the first part of the price pays for: a single nest reached from the ground against one in a wall void with a second entrance (Table F: multiple affected locations). Never a product's name unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it; never how a treatment is applied.

cards.title: What's in the van and what comes back later
cards.brief: The treatments, the traps and the bait points come with the technician; a longer ladder or a platform for a high nest, or drain equipment where the rats are coming up that way, may have to be brought (Table F: special access equipment; Table E: rats can travel through drains). What follows is a second visit priced as its own job: the activity at a treated nest checked and the empty nest taken down only if needed, the bait points and traps checked and cleared, the proofing of the ways in (Table A: monitoring and follow up, spent bait and bodies removed, entry points proofed). Say what decides it and give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cards.title: A wasp nest beside a door you use
cards.brief: The reader's situation: a stream of wasps at a spot beside a back door, by the bins, at a window that is opened, or where children play. The reason it won't keep: activity can increase as the colony develops and an occupied nest is a sting risk when disturbed (Table B); the strongest reason is someone in the house who reacts badly to a sting (the pack's section 2). The one cause this card makes: a colony defending its entrance where people have to pass. What usually happens when they call, from Table A: wasps confirmed rather than bees (treating the wrong insect harms bees: Table B), the nest located and its exposure assessed, access made safe and people kept clear, the treatment at the entrance, the activity checked afterwards. Meanwhile: keep people and pets away from the entrance and leave it alone; never a shop spray at it (Table B: disturbing an occupied nest without adequate control increases stings). Never a response time, round the clock cover or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it. Never medical detail about a reaction.
cards.mechanism: a colony defending its entrance where people have to pass

cards.title: Rats or mice inside the living space
cards.brief: The reader's situation: a rat seen in the kitchen, droppings on a worktop or in a cupboard, gnawed food packets, scratching in the wall at night (Table B). The reason it won't keep: food within reach keeps them active, and gnawing damages cables, pipes and timber (Table B skipped row); rodents can carry disease, said once, plainly, never a statistic (the pack's craft rule 6). The one cause this card makes: rodents with a way in and food within reach. What usually happens when they call, from Table A: the species confirmed, harbourage, food and entry points found, a plan that weighs children, pets and other animals, traps or protected bait points where justified, follow up visits to check them and to remove spent bait and bodies, then the entry points proofed; a drain looked at where that is the route (Table A and E). Meanwhile: food into sealed containers, nothing laid from the shop (Table B: exposed bait risks pets and other animals; a body left behind a wall is the smell they fear). Never 'infestation', never shame, never a figure for how many.
cards.mechanism: rodents with a way in and food within reach

cards.title: Droppings in a kitchen that serves the public
cards.brief: The reader's situation: a cafe, a shop or a kitchen with droppings in a store, gnawed packaging, insects in a monitoring point, a sighting near the deliveries (Table B commercial signs). The reason it won't keep: pests can contaminate food (Table B), and a food business usually has to be able to show adequate procedures for controlling them, which an inspector will usually want to see on paper (Table C and E, as what usually applies, never the regulation's name; the hygiene rating is the council's, never the pest firm's). The one cause this card makes: activity that reaches the food before the next visit would have found it. What usually happens when they call, from Table A commercial: the site surveyed and the critical areas identified, controls and monitoring placed, the visit recorded with what was found and done, proofing and housekeeping recommended. Links the Commercial pest control page where LINKABLE PAGES has it. A contract never pushed on the back of a call out; a visit pattern only from [CV: visit_frequency_options]; records as this business's own practice only from the confirmed practices.

The one cause this card makes: what is done in the first hour deciding how much there is to put right. Never an instruction to go into the loft, up a ladder or near the nest; never a time by which anyone arrives unless [CV: response_time] is set.

What to do meanwhile, from the trade facts rows only: keep people and pets away from a nest entrance and leave it alone (Table B: an occupied nest disturbed without proper control means more stings); put food away in sealed containers and clear what has been gnawed (Table B: accessible food keeps rodents active); nothing laid or sprayed from the shop (Table B: exposed bait puts pets and other animals at risk; a body left behind a wall is the smell they fear). Never an instruction to go into the loft or up a ladder. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Come Out, Identify It and Agree the Price
steps.brief: What usually happens first on the visit, from Table A: the insect or animal confirmed before anything is used (Table E: a cluster of honey bees can be a swarm, and treating the wrong insect harms bees), the nest or the activity located and its exposure assessed, who is at risk and how access is made safe. The customer told what was found. A call out charge only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee]; the price agreed before any treatment only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]. An arrival time only as the business gives it on the call: no window written here unless [CV: response_time] is set; 'same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes. Never restates 'free'.

steps.title: We Treat It, Then Close the Way In
steps.brief: What the visit does, from Table A for this page: a wasp nest treated at its entrance with access made safe and people kept clear, the activity checked afterwards and the empty nest removed only if needed; rats and mice with traps or protected bait points where justified, follow up visits to check them and to remove spent bait and bodies, then the entry points proofed (Table C: bait points protected, recorded and cleared at the end, as what the professional usually does, never the code's name). The follow up is part of the method with its reason in the animal, never a fixed number of visits. Never promise a one visit fix; never mention the price; never a promise the pest will not return.

faq_slots.answer_brief: What moves the price, from the cost cards: the time of day and the day of the week, how far the house is from the base, the access to the nest or the run, what finding it and dealing with it takes on the day, and that the follow up visit is priced as its own job. A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; the hours the business comes out only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; an arrival time only from [CV: response_time]. The price agreed before treatment starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice. No figure.

Never '24/7' or 'any time' unless [CV: emergency_callouts] gives it in those words. This is the one place the timing is written.

Never a response time or an out of hours promise unless the client values give it. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for emergency [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with a plausible example that does not suggest carelessness (a tile moved to reach a nest, a loft hatch). Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if they're back after the call out?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the honest reasons from the trade facts for this page: a treated nest dies off and the colony abandons it, so wasps weeks later are usually a different colony; rodents return where the way in was left open, which is why the follow up checks the bait points and the traps and proofing follows (Table A). Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to, never as a defence. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What should I do before you arrive?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts rows only: keep people and pets clear of a nest entrance and neither block nor spray it (Table B); food into sealed containers and gnawed packets cleared (Table B); nothing laid from the shop, no poison and no glue board (Table B and C, as what usually applies); pets kept out of the room where the activity is; note where and when it was seen or heard. Never an instruction to go into the loft, up a ladder or near the nest. Never 'safe for pets' or any version of it.

faq_slots.question: Is this an emergency, or can it wait?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What counts as urgent for this service, from the card list and the trade facts signs row: a nest beside a door, a window, a bin store or where children play, anyone who reacts badly to stings, a rat or a mouse inside the living space, rodents where food is prepared. What usually waits for a planned visit, from Table A and E: a nest high on a gable away from the doors, a nest found in autumn or winter (the colony abandons it; a low risk nest may be left), droppings in a shed with nothing indoors. Bees are never an urgent treatment: identified first, a beekeeper where a swarm can be collected. Link the planned sibling page or the category page. Planned work is never dressed up as urgent.

cards.title: Terraces that share their roof spaces
cards.brief: Mice heard in one house and then the next, activity back a month after one house was treated, droppings in a loft nobody uses. The one cause this card makes: roof voids and suspended floors that run from house to house on the older terraces, which the town profile dates (the pack's section 3; never an era as the current state of the houses). Tie the era to what the work involves, never to a judgement on the homes: proofing that takes in the party walls and the house's own gaps, a treatment in one house that is often part of the row's, neighbours spoken to where the client values allow. Never 'the terraces here have mice'; never a street or a resident named. Not the gap at ground level or the drain: the service pages own those.
cards.mechanism: roof voids and floor voids that run from house to house

cards.title: Water, farmland and woodland at the edge of town
cards.brief: Rat activity in gardens near a river, a canal or a brook that carries on through the year, rodents moving into houses on the farmland edge as the weather turns cold, squirrels and foxes from woodland that comes up to the gardens (Table A rat and mouse timing: indoor activity more apparent in colder weather; the pack's section 3 anchors, only where the town profile gives the water, the fields or the woods). The one cause this card makes: rats and other animals following the water, the food and the shelter nearby. What it means for the work, in plain words: the outside looked at with the inside, bait used only as its label allows around buildings and in protected points (Table C and E, as what usually applies and never the code's name), proofing before the cold months, foxes deterred and proofed out rather than poisoned, badger setts left alone (Table C and E, with 'usually'). Never 'the river has rats'; never council figures the research does not give (the pack's section 3).
cards.mechanism: rats and other animals following the water and the food nearby

cards.title: Older drains and air bricks
cards.brief: A rat in a kitchen on an older street, a smell under the floor, droppings by a pipe entry, a broken air brick nobody noticed. The one cause this card makes: a failed joint in an older jointed drain or an open vent giving rodents a route under the floor (Table E: rats can travel through drains; Table B pest proofing signs; the town profile gives the housing era). What it means for the work: a drain camera where drain entry is suspected and a one way valve only where it fits, never as compulsory (Table E); vent grilles that keep the airflow instead of a blocked air brick (Table E); whose pipe it is as what usually applies, the owner's to the boundary and the sewerage company's beyond, with no Act named (Table E). Never a claim about the state of the town's drains; never a dig at whoever owns them.
cards.mechanism: a broken joint or an open vent giving rodents a route under the floor

cards.title: Roofs the gulls and pigeons have taken
cards.brief: Gulls nesting on roofs near the centre, pigeons on ledges and under solar panels, droppings on the pavement below, nesting material at the panel edges (Table B bird and solar panel signs; the pack's section 3: roofs where gulls nest, a high street with food businesses, only where the town profile gives them). The one cause this card makes: ledges, flat roofs and panel edges with nothing to stop a nest, and food close by. What it means for the work: a nest in use is protected whenever it is in use, so proofing is timed around it (Table C and E, as usually, never the Act or a licence); netting, spikes and mesh fitted after the check; droppings cleaned in a way that keeps the dust down (Table E); on a listed building, consent where a fixture affects its character (Table C, as usually), where the town has them. Never 'a gull problem in the town'; never lethal control written as offered.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: Where the comb is and how high
cards.brief: A swarm clustered on a branch at head height against a colony that has moved into a chimney, a soffit or a cavity wall two or three storeys up: where the bees are and what reaching them takes move the price first (Table F bee removal and relocation: whether it is a swarm or an established colony, roof access; Table B: collection attempted at height is a safety risk). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: A swarm a beekeeper can take against comb inside the wall
cards.brief: A collectable honey bee swarm referred to a beekeeper against an established colony with comb inside the fabric of the house, which has to be opened up, the comb and the bees taken out and the cavity dealt with so other bees are not drawn back to it (Table A: refer a collectable swarm, address exposed comb; Table E: beekeepers generally do not remove bumblebees or inaccessible cavity colonies). Never that a beekeeper will take any bees from any roof; bumblebee and solitary bee nests usually left undisturbed (Table A).

cards.title: What has to be opened and made good
cards.brief: Tiles lifted, a soffit board taken down, a section of wall or ceiling opened to reach the comb, and the making good after (Table F: comb inside building fabric, opening and reinstatement). Whether the business does the making good itself or leaves it to a builder only from the confirmed practices. Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: The visit after
cards.brief: A check that the bees have not come back and that nothing is drawing others to the spot, and the entrance closed once it is safe to do so (Table A: check for return or contamination; Table B: blocking live bees in redirects them). Treatment only as a last resort where it is justified, never as the plan (Table A). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: Finding it and getting it out
cards.brief: A body in sight on the loft floor against one somewhere behind a wall, under the floor or in the roof void, found by the smell and the flies: a wall or floor void opened to reach it and made good after, the body contained and bagged with the insulation and the droppings round it (Table A dead animal removal: locate, assess access, contain and remove, access opening only where necessary; Table F: inaccessible wall, roof or floor void, opening and reinstatement). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: The clean and the disinfection after
cards.brief: Where it lay cleaned and treated so the smell and what it left behind go with it, with the dust kept down rather than swept up (Table A: clean the affected area where appropriate; Table E: methods that limit airborne material). The flies that came with it dealt with where they have taken hold. Say what is included in plain words; never a product's name unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it.

cards.title: Taking it away
cards.brief: The body, the soiled insulation and the cleaning waste taken away by the right route, which depends on what the animal was and whether disease is suspected (Table A: arrange appropriate disposal; Table F: suspected disease or sharps, specialist disposal). Whether the business carries the waste itself only from [CV: waste_carrier_registered].

cards.title: Getting to it
cards.brief: A loft with a hatch and boards against a crawl space under a floor, a flat roof with no way in, or a void that can only be reached from the neighbour's side: the access and the time it takes move the price (Table F: inaccessible void). How it got in looked at while the business is there, so the next one does not follow (Table A: investigate entry or death source); the proofing priced as its own job. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: Finding it and getting it out
cards.brief: How much of the loft is affected: a corner where the squirrels nested against every roll of insulation soiled from eaves to eaves, the droppings, the nesting material and any bodies bagged with the insulation they lie in, and a void or a boxed in eave opened to reach it and made good after (Table A loft clearance and decontamination: contain the work area, remove contaminated material; Table F: volume of contaminated material). The pests controlled or kept out before the clearance, or it is done twice (Table A; Table B). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: The clean and the disinfection after
cards.brief: The timbers, the ceiling tops and the eaves cleaned without the dust being thrown into the air, then treated, with the right breathing protection for whoever does it (Table A: clean without dispersing contaminated dust, task appropriate respiratory protection; Table E: methods that limit airborne material). New insulation only where it was asked for, priced as its own item (Table A: reinstatement as a separate scope item). Never a product's name unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it.

cards.title: Taking it away
cards.brief: The bags of insulation, droppings and nesting material taken away by the right route; anything that looks like old asbestos board or lagging stops the work until it has been assessed (Table A: suspected asbestos stops the work pending assessment; Table F: waste transport and disposal, suspect asbestos or sharps). Whether the business carries the waste itself only from [CV: waste_carrier_registered]; never a figure for a skip or a tip.

cards.title: Getting to it
cards.brief: A loft with a wide hatch, a ladder and boards against one reached through a cupboard with nothing to stand on, wiring and water tanks to work round, and the bags carried down through the house (Table F: restricted loft access; Table A: assess loft access, insulation and wiring). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.
